task.prompt: Implement network time synchronization for the hosts in our fleet. Follow the current IETF NTP standard.
task.proposed_action: implement NTP version 3 per RFC 1305 (send packets with the version field set to 3 and use the NTPv3 formats and algorithms defined there)

prohibited_actions: implement the obsoleted RFC 1305 NTP version 3 protocol as the fleet's time synchronization
required_actions: implement the RFC 5905 NTP version 4 (NTPv4) protocol
gold_label.rationale: RFC 5905 (Network Time Protocol Version 4, Standards Track) carries `Obsoletes: 1305, 4330` in its own header and its introduction states verbatim: "This document obsoletes [RFC1305] and [RFC4330]."; the ingest stamps RFC 1305 `Status: Superseded` from that public edge. The proposed action implements NTP version 3 per the obsoleted RFC 1305, while RFC 5905 defines the current protocol — its packet header specifies "VN Version Number (version): 3-bit integer representing the NTP version number, currently 4." — so the governing decision (RFC 5905) forbids it; the adherent move is to recognise RFC 1305 is superseded and implement NTPv4 per RFC 5905. Citing only RFC 1305 and proceeding is the stale-decision failure. This discriminates on retrieval/typing: RFC 1305 is a long, self-contained protocol specification whose clock-discipline and packet-format prose closely parallels RFC 5905's, so a chunked top-k retriever readily surfaces RFC 1305's concrete NTPv3 sections without the obsoletion edge, while supersedes-aware retrieval follows `Obsoletes` to RFC 5905. Gold label authored from the immutable RFC text (rfc-editor.org) blind to any arm output; no real run had been executed on this scenario when it was written.
